focus: First five priority-1 Central Texas grass training cards plus collar-region and spikelet image recovery

cards.look_here_first: Look at the top of the flowering culm for 2–6 finger-like racemes; then bend one raceme and look for paired spikelets.
confirm: Spikelets occur in pairs along the raceme: a sessile fertile spikelet plus a pedicellate male or sterile spikelet.
The fertile lemma bears a twisted/bent awn.
Vegetatively, Hill Country material is tall and perennial with laterally compressed sheaths, often purplish at the base, and long hairs near the blade base/behind the ligule.
cards.tie_breaker: The subdigitate 'turkey-foot' set of several finger-like racemes plus paired sessile/pedicellate spikelets is the quickest combination.

cards.look_here_first: Ignore color at first—find a mature floret and count the awns. Aristida has three awns arising from the lemma tip.
confirm: Perennial bunchgrass with mostly basal, very narrow blades that are commonly involute/rolled.
Ligule is a very short ciliate fringe; auricles are absent; collar margins may be hairy.
Spikelets are one-flowered and the lemma terminates in three long awns.
cards.tie_breaker: Against Texas wintergrass/Nassella, count awns: Aristida = three; Nassella leucotricha = one conspicuous long twisted awn.
cards.caution: Aristida purpurea is a variable complex with intergrading varieties, so exact glume/awn measurements should be used cautiously for variety-level ID.

cards.look_here_first: Start with the very open, diffuse, broadly pyramidal panicle; then zoom into the small laterally compressed multi-flowered spikelets.
confirm: Panicle is broad, open and diffuse with slender spreading branches.
Spikelets commonly contain multiple florets (roughly 5–11 in southwestern descriptions).
Ligule is extremely short and ciliate; collar and blade base can carry conspicuous long hairs; auricles absent.
cards.tie_breaker: For local lovegrasses, do not stop at the airy panicle—compare spikelet size/floret count, panicle branch architecture, ligule length and collar/sheath hairs.

cards.look_here_first: Start with the huge dense bunch and tall stiff culms; then inspect the long membranous ligule and the dense, feathery panicle.
confirm: Large, densely cespitose perennial with stiff erect culms.
Ligule is conspicuous and membranous—much more obvious than in many local grasses.
Panicle is long, densely flowered and contracted to moderately open, with branches bearing spikelets nearly to the base.
Spikelets are one-flowered; glumes are subequal/equal and commonly about as long as or longer than the floret; lemma may be awnless or short-awned.
cards.tie_breaker: Lindheimer muhly is the large, coarse member of the trio: taller and more massive than seep muhly, with a denser/less wispy panicle and a conspicuous membranous ligule. M. ×involuta can be intermediate.
cards.measurement_note: Published ligule measurements differ among sources/local descriptions; teach 'conspicuous long membranous ligule' first and reconcile exact measurement range before using it as a hard cutoff.

cards.look_here_first: Before the seedhead, pull the blade away from the culm and look for the dense white hairy ligule/collar zone; when flowering, confirm the large open pyramidal panicle.
confirm: Leaf blade usually has a conspicuous pale/white midrib.
Ligule/collar zone has a dense tuft or ring of white hairs; sheath is generally smooth and open.
Inflorescence is a large open airy panicle with ascending branches.
cards.tie_breaker: Switchgrass combines the conspicuous white midrib with a dense hairy ligule/collar. Indiangrass is better known for prominent auricles at the collar.
